 Washington D. C. iGaming bill faces year-end deadline as council weighs 25% tax 
 2026-11-17 · 13:19 
 United States 
 Reading time 2:37 min 
 Washington D.C. lawmakers are preparing to consider legislation that would legalize online casinos, impose a 25% tax on adjusted gross gaming revenue and restrict unregulated sweepstakes operators,  although a limited legislative calendar could prevent the measure from becoming law before the end of 2026.
 The Internet Gaming and Consumer Protection Act of 2026, introduced by Councilmember Wendell Felder (D-Ward 7) in April, is scheduled for consideration by the Council of the District of Columbia's Committee on Human Services on Wednesday, November 18. 
 The committee is expected to mark up Bill B26-0656 , which has remained under its consideration since its introduction. The proposed legislation would allow online and mobile casino gambling for individuals aged 21 and older, with no limit on the number of licensed operators. Companies would pay an initial licensing fee of $2 million and a renewal fee of $500,000.
 In addition to the proposed 25% tax on adjusted gross internet gaming revenue, operators would contribute 2% to a new iGaming Community Reinvestment Fund intended to support problem gambling treatment programs in the region.
 The legislation would also establish a regulatory framework for sweepstakes casinos, prohibiting unregulated operations while allowing licensed companies to offer such games. Sweepstakes casinos typically operate using a dual-currency system, which has complicated regulatory efforts in jurisdictions introducing real-money online gambling.
 Oversight would fall to the Office of Lottery and Gaming (OLG), which currently regulates the District's lottery, charitable gaming and sports betting activities. T he agency operates under the oversight of the Committee on Human Services.
 However, the bill faces a compressed legislative timetable. If approved by the committee, it must pass two separate readings and secure majority support in the full Council. Only three legislative sessions remain scheduled for 2026, on November 24, December 1 and December 15. 
 The legislation would then require approval from Mayor Muriel Bowser (D), who has 10 days to sign or veto it. An approved measure would subsequently undergo a mandatory 30-day congressional review , during which federal lawmakers could block it through a joint resolution, although such intervention is uncommon.
 Any legislation that remains unpassed when the current Council period ends will expire , placing the bill's prospects for enactment before the end of 2026 in doubt.
 The proposal follows Washington, DC's legalization of sports betting in 2018. The District currently has six regulated mobile sportsbook operators , including FanDuel, BetMGM and DraftKings, some or all of which could seek online casino licenses if the legislation passes.
 Unlike jurisdictions such as Florida, where disputes involving tribal gaming interests have affected sports betting regulation, the District does not face comparable tribal casino restrictions. 
 If enacted, the measure would introduce regulated online slots and roulette to Washington, DC, where offshore casino platforms are already accessible. The District would join eight states identified as permitting online casino gambling: Michigan, New Jersey, West Virginia, Connecticut, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maine and Rhode Island.
 Maine has also pursued restrictions on sweepstakes casinos, legalizing online casinos in January before moving to outlaw sweepstakes sites in July. Unlike Maine's sequential approach, the District's proposal would establish online casino regulation and restrictions on unlicensed sweepstakes operations simultaneously.
 The Washington, DC, proposal has drawn competing views over whether legalization would improve consumer protection or expand gambling-related harm. During a public hearing in May, Les Bernal, director of Stop Predatory Gambling, disputed industry arguments that regulated gambling reduces illegal activity.
 “The narrative behind illegal gambling was a made-up public relations narrative by the gambling industry, and the reason why they needed to do it is because your constituents weren’t demanding commercial sports gambling. They sure as heck aren’t demanding online casino gambling. They had to create this phony public relations narrative to breathe life into a lobbying campaign ,” Bernal said.
 Michelle MacGregor, representing the Sports Betting Alliance, a lobbying organization supporting legal online sports betting and iGaming, argued that regulation would shift existing gambling activity toward licensed platforms. 
 “ Legalizing iGaming is not a question of whether District residents will play these games. They already are ,” said MacGregor.
